title: Modern Scheduling with systemd Timers
description: Create the app-maintenance.service and app-maintenance.timer unit files that schedule daily maintenance at 03:00.
scenario: Your team is migrating from cron to systemd timers. For the maintenance script at /usr/local/bin/maintenance.sh, create the unit pair: /etc/systemd/system/app-maintenance.service (a oneshot service running the script) and /etc/systemd/system/app-maintenance.timer (fires daily at 03:00, with Persistent=true so a missed run happens at boot, enabled via timers.target).
symptoms: No app-maintenance.service or app-maintenance.timer units exist
The migration plan requires Persistent=true so missed runs recover
The timer must hook into timers.target to be startable at boot
mission: Create /etc/systemd/system/app-maintenance.service (Type=oneshot, ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/maintenance.sh) and /etc/systemd/system/app-maintenance.timer (OnCalendar daily at 03:00, Persistent=true, WantedBy=timers.target).

hints.title: Unit pair naming
hints.content: The timer foo.timer automatically triggers foo.service — the names must match, which is why both start with app-maintenance.

hints.title: OnCalendar syntax
hints.content: `OnCalendar=*-*-* 03:00:00` means every day at 03:00 (the keyword `daily` is equivalent). Calendar events beat the old five-field cron syntax for readability.

hints.title: Persistent=true
hints.content: Without it, a server powered off at 03:00 skips the run forever. Persistent catches up on the next boot.

hints.title: The [Install] section
hints.content: `WantedBy=timers.target` is what makes `systemctl enable app-maintenance.timer` work at boot.

acceptance_criteria.description: the timer is Persistent and wired to timers.target
